pos: n. (the right of presenting a clergyman to a vacant parish benefice; in English law a property right, which could be inherited, granted or sold)
etymology: Anglo-French avoeson, from Latin advocatio, a calling to, from advocare, to summon or call in; the patron was the advocatus of the church.
biblical_def: An advowson is the right to name the minister of a parish. In English law it was real property: it descended with a manor, could be sold apart from the land, could be mortgaged, and was litigated in the royal courts. Monasteries accumulated advowsons in hundreds, because the right to present carried with it the power to appropriate the tithes and leave a poorly paid vicar in charge. The arrangement survived the Reformation and parts of it survive still. The New Testament says nothing about such a right and a good deal about the appointment of ministers, and the pattern is uniformly ecclesiastical rather than proprietary. “when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord” (Act 14:23). Titus is left in Crete to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) by a stated standard of character. And the final appointment is not in human hands at all: “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines advowson as a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice; and patron as one who has the gift of a benefice, one who protects or supports.
webster_full: ADVOWSON, n. In English law, a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice. Advowson signifies taking into protection, and is synonymous with patronage.
PATRON, n. In the church of England and of Rome, one who has the gift and disposition of a benefice; a protector; a defender.
PRESENT, v.t. To nominate to an ecclesiastical benefice; to offer to the bishop or ordinary as a candidate for institution.
BENEFICE, n. In the middle ages, benefice was used for a fee. In church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.
INDUCTION, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the giving a clerk possession of a benefice, after institution.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
corruption_summary: The right to name a parish's minister, held as property and sold like land.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the ownership of a pulpit. Once the right to present is property, the man presented is chosen by whoever holds the deed, for whatever reasons property owners have; younger sons were placed in livings they never visited, and the congregation had no voice in either case. It is not simony, because the office itself was not sold, only the right to fill it — a distinction the law maintained carefully and the sheep could not detect.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the qualifications for the ministry are stated and testable, and that they are about the man: “For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre” (Tit 1:7). Where a church cannot examine a man against that list before he is set over it, the list is a dead letter whatever is written in the parish register.
roots_summary: Latin advocatio, a calling in; Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint or ordain; Greek kathistemi (G2525), to set in place; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek peripoieomai (G4046), to purchase.
roots_lines: Latin advocare — to call in; the patron as the church's advocatus.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to ordain; “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23).
Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to appoint, to set in office; “and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).
Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to acquire, to purchase; “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
usage: “and had prayed with fasting” (Act 14:23) — how the apostolic church filled a vacancy.
“as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7) — the man is a steward, not a tenant.
“Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — the charge no deed conveys.

pos: n. (the stipend or estate set apart to maintain a canon of a cathedral or collegiate church; also the office so endowed)
etymology: Medieval Latin praebenda, things to be furnished, from praebere, to supply — the allowance provided to a canon.
biblical_def: A prebend is the endowment attached to a stall in a cathedral: usually a named manor, parish or portion of tithe whose revenue maintained one canon, who held the stall for life and drew the income whether or not he resided. The system funded the English cathedrals for eight hundred years and funded a great deal of absence with them. The principle of a settled maintenance for ministers is not a medieval invention; it is Mosaic and apostolic. “I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21) establishes it in the law, and Paul argues straight from that precedent: “they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple” (1Co 9:13), and therefore “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14). The word ordained there is not advisory. What the law and the apostle both attach to the maintenance is service, and that is the clause a prebend made detachable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prebend as the stipend or maintenance granted out of the estate of a cathedral or collegiate church; and stipend as settled pay or compensation for services.
webster_full: PREBEND, n. The stipend or maintenance granted out of the estate of a cathedral or collegiate church, usually in consideration of a duty to be performed.
STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
STALL, n. A seat enclosed in a choir; the seat of a dignified clergyman in the choir of a cathedral.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling dower on a woman. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a public institution.
scriptures: And, behold, I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve, even the service of the tabernacle of the congregation.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?
corruption_summary: The endowment attached to a cathedral stall, drawn for life whether the holder served or not.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the separation of the stipend from the service, which the prebendal system made structurally easy: the revenue came from a named estate, the duty was discharged by a hired vicar choral, and the canon could be in another county or another kingdom. The law never contemplated it. “for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21) makes the tenth the wage of actual work, and the Levite who did not serve had no claim on it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's, who establishes the right and then declines to use it, which is the strongest possible way to hold both halves. His argument for the right is unanswerable — “If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?” (1Co 9:11) — and his refusal of it at Corinth was so that nothing should hinder the gospel. A maintenance is a just due and never a possession.
roots_summary: Latin praebenda, things to be supplied; Hebrew maaser (H4643), a tenth; Hebrew abodah (H5656), service; Greek thusiasterion (G2379), an altar; Greek diatasso (G1299), to ordain or appoint.
roots_lines: Latin praebere — to supply, to furnish; whence praebenda, a prebend.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tenth, a tithe; “all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance” (Num 18:21).
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — labour, service; “for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21).
Greek thusiasterion (G2379) — an altar; “they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar” (1Co 9:13).
Greek diatasso (G1299) — to arrange, to ordain; “hath the Lord ordained” (1Co 9:14).
usage: “for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21) — the clause a prebend detached.
“should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14) — the right, plainly stated.
“is it a great thing” (1Co 9:11) — the argument Paul made and then waived.

pos: n. (the holder of a prebend; a canon of a cathedral drawing the revenue of a named stall)
etymology: Medieval Latin praebendarius, one who holds a praebenda — the man attached to the stipend.
biblical_def: A prebendary is the man in the stall. At its best the office supported learned clergy who preached, taught, governed dioceses and produced much of English theology; a great many of the divines whose books survive were prebendaries. At its worst the title attached to a boy, a courtier or a foreign cardinal who never saw the cathedral and whose duty was performed by a substitute paid a fraction of the revenue. Scripture makes a distinction within the ministry that bears directly on this: “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17). Double honour is maintenance as well as respect, and it is attached to two things, ruling well and labouring. The proof text Paul then cites is agricultural and leaves no room for the absentee: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18). An ox that is not treading is not being muzzled.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prebendary as an ecclesiastic who enjoys a prebend; and sinecure as an ecclesiastical benefice without cure of souls, an office which has revenue without employment.
webster_full: PREBENDARY, n. An ecclesiastic who enjoys a prebend; the incumbent of a prebend.
SINECURE, n. An ecclesiastical benefice without cure of souls. An office which has revenue without employment.
INCUMBENT, n. A person who is in present possession of a benefice or of any office.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time. In the ecclesiastical sense, the abode of a parson on his benefice.
DEPUTY, n. A person appointed or elected to act for another, especially a person sent with a special commission to act in the place of another.
scriptures: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The man in the stall, sometimes a great divine and sometimes an absentee boy with a substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sinecure, a word Webster defines with the church in view: revenue without employment, a benefice without cure of souls. The medieval and early modern abuse was systematic, and its victims were parishes. Jeremiah's woe is addressed to exactly this class: “Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD” (Jer 23:1) — and scattering is what happens when nobody is there.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the necessity Paul felt, which is the opposite of a sinecure in every respect: “for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!” (1Co 9:16). A man who holds a ministry as an income has not merely failed a duty; he has taken a title that, in the apostle's mouth, carries a woe for not doing the thing itself.
roots_summary: Latin praebendarius, a prebend-holder; Greek time (G5092), honour or price; Greek kopiao (G2872), to labour to weariness; Greek phimoo (G5392), to muzzle; Hebrew raah (H7462), to shepherd.
roots_lines: Latin praebendarius — the holder of a prebend.
Greek time (G5092) — honour, and also price or payment; “counted worthy of double honour” (1Ti 5:17).
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to toil, to labour to weariness; “especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17).
Greek phimoo (G5392) — to muzzle; “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn” (1Ti 5:18).
Greek anagke (G318) — necessity, constraint; “for necessity is laid upon me” (1Co 9:16).
usage: “the elders that rule well” (1Ti 5:17) — honour attached to performance.
“The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18) — the labourer, specifically.
“that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture” (Jer 23:1) — the woe on absentees.

pos: n. (a clergyman living in community under a rule — usually the Rule of Augustine — while serving churches and administering sacraments; distinguished from both a monk and a secular canon)
etymology: Latin canonicus regularis, a canon living under a regula or rule, from Greek kanon, a measuring rod or standard.
biblical_def: A canon regular is a clergyman under vows and a rule who nevertheless exercises a public ministry: he preaches, hears confessions and serves the parishes his house owns, which a monk properly so called does not. The Augustinian canons, the Premonstratensians and the Victorines were all of this kind, and they were the medieval church's most serious attempt at a disciplined, educated, resident pastoral clergy. What the arrangement could not do was keep its rule from hardening into the thing Paul warned the Colossians about. His description of a rule-based religion is precise and devastating: it consists in “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21), and such things “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23). The charge is not that the regulations are harsh but that they are powerless against the flesh while looking impressive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regular as instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline, belonging to a monastic order; and rule as an established principle, a governing direction for conduct.
webster_full: REGULAR, a. Instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline. Belonging to a monastic order; as regular clergy, in distinction from the secular clergy.
RULE, n. Government; sway; control. An established principle or axiom; that which is prescribed as a guide to conduct.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend. A law or rule in ecclesiastical matters.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God. A promise of something to be given or done hereafter.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
scriptures: Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances,
corruption_summary: Clergy under a rule serving real parishes, and the apostle's verdict on regulations that cannot touch the flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the rule that becomes a gospel. Paul does not deny that ascetic regulation produces an appearance of wisdom; he grants it and says that is all it produces. The question he puts to the Colossians is one every rule-keeping community must answer: “if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20). A man under vows who has not answered it is governed by the very thing his vows were meant to escape.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the liberty that Scripture treats as a thing to be defended rather than enjoyed quietly: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1). The canons regular were right that a disciplined, educated, resident clergy is a great good. Discipline freely chosen is not bondage; a rule that is required for acceptance with God is.
roots_summary: Greek kanon (G2583), a rule or measuring rod; Greek dogmatizo (G1379), to be subject to ordinances; Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship; Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek zugos (G2218), a yoke.
roots_lines: Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, a standard; whence canon.
Greek dogmatizo (G1379) — to be subject to decrees; “are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20).
Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-chosen worship; “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23).
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; “Stand fast therefore in the liberty” (Gal 5:1).
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke; “the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1).
usage: “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21) — Paul quoting a rule to dismiss it.
“not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23) — the verdict on austerity.
“be not entangled again” (Gal 5:1) — the standing danger of a rule.

pos: n. (clergy who live in the world and serve parishes and cathedrals, as distinguished from the regular clergy who live under a monastic rule)
etymology: Latin clerus saecularis, from saeculum, an age or the present world — clergy of this age, living among ordinary people.
biblical_def: The secular clergy are the parish priests, vicars, curates, deans and secular canons: men in orders who live in the saeculum, the present age, among families and markets and harvests, rather than in a cloister. For most of the Middle Ages they were the poorer, less educated and less celebrated half of the clergy, and the long quarrel between seculars and regulars — over preaching rights, burial fees and confessions — fills the records of every diocese. Scripture gives the seculars the better position without deciding the quarrel. Paul's instruction is not to leave the world but to hold it loosely: “they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away” (1Co 7:31). Titus states the goal of grace as a manner of living in exactly this place: “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12). The adverbs do the work, and all three describe a man with neighbours.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secular as pertaining to this present world or to things not spiritual, and among catholics, not bound by monastic vows; and parish as the precinct and inhabitants belonging to and attending a church.
webster_full: SECULAR, a. Pertaining to this present world, or to things not spiritual or holy; relating to things not immediately or primarily respecting the soul. Among catholics, not regular; not bound by monastic vows.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
CURATE, n. A clergyman in the church of England, employed to perform divine service in the place of the incumbent.
VICAR, n. The incumbent of an appropriated or impropriated benefice.
LAITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.
scriptures: And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
corruption_summary: The clergy who live in the world among families and markets, and the apostolic instruction for exactly that place.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the two-tier Christianity that the words themselves encode: a religious life for those under vows and a merely secular one for everyone else, with the implication that the second is a concession. Paul knows no such tiers. His rule for every calling is the same: “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24) — the farmer, the slave, the married man and the parish priest all abide with God where they are.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the world is the place of obedience and not an obstacle to it. Our Lord prayed “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15), which settles the geography. What must be held loosely is not the neighbour or the harvest but the permanence of the arrangement, since “the fashion of this world passeth away” (1Co 7:31).
roots_summary: Latin saeculum, an age or the world; Greek kosmos (G2889), the world; Greek schema (G4976), the fashion or outward form; Greek chraomai (G5530), to use; Greek sophronos (G4996), soberly.
roots_lines: Latin saeculum — an age, this present world; whence secular.
Greek chraomai (G5530) — to use, to make use of; “they that use this world, as not abusing it” (1Co 7:31).
Greek schema (G4976) — outward fashion, form; “for the fashion of this world passeth away” (1Co 7:31).
Greek sophronos (G4996) — soberly, with sound mind; “we should live soberly, righteously, and godly” (Tit 2:12).
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain; “therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24).
usage: “as not abusing it” (1Co 7:31) — the whole discipline of a secular calling.
“in this present world” (Tit 2:12) — where godliness is to be practised.
“wherein he is called” (1Co 7:24) — no higher tier to transfer into.

pos: n. (clergy living under a monastic or canonical rule — monks, canons regular and friars in orders — as distinguished from the secular clergy)
etymology: Latin clerus regularis, clergy under a regula or rule; the Latin regula is a straight-edge, a ruler, whence both rule and regular.
biblical_def: The regular clergy are those in holy orders who also live under a rule: Benedictines, Cistercians, canons regular, and the friars who were ordained. The distinction from the seculars is not one of sanctity but of government — a regular answers to an abbot or a provincial as well as to a bishop, which is why the two classes spent four centuries litigating about jurisdiction. The vocabulary is worth holding onto, because rule in the New Testament is a surveyor's term for a line to walk along, not a fence to be kept inside. Paul pronounces his benediction on those who use one: “as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God” (Gal 6:16) — and the rule in question is the preceding verse, that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails but a new creature. He says the same to the Philippians: “whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing” (Php 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regular as governed by rule, belonging to a monastic order; and discipline as instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the correction of manners.
webster_full: REGULAR, a. Governed by rule or rules; steady or uniform in a course or practice. Belonging to a monastic order.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the regulation of practice. Correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
ORDER, n. A religious fraternity; as the order of Benedictines. Regularity; settled mode of operation.
PROVINCIAL, n. One belonging to a province. An ecclesiastical governor over a province or district.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.
scriptures: And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
corruption_summary: Clergy under a rule as well as a bishop, and the New Testament sense of rule as a line to walk along.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the multiplication of jurisdictions, which is what the regular-secular quarrel actually was: two chains of command over the same souls, each able to overrule the other, with the laity as the contested revenue. The gospel is indifferent to the organisational question and ruthless about the doctrinal one, which is why Paul's rule is a single sentence of content: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature” (Gal 6:15).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that personal discipline is apostolic and is not the same thing as a rule imposed for merit. Paul kept one, in athletic terms and for a stated reason: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway” (1Co 9:27). That is self-discipline in the service of a ministry, which no Reformed reader should sneer at, and it is not a vow taken to acquire standing before God.
roots_summary: Latin regula, a straight-edge or rule; Greek kanon (G2583), a rule; Greek stoicheo (G4748), to walk in line; Greek ktisis (G2937), a creation; Greek doulagogeo (G1396), to bring into subjection.
roots_lines: Latin regula — a straight-edge; whence both rule and regular.
Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, a rule; “as many as walk according to this rule” (Gal 6:16).
Greek stoicheo (G4748) — to walk in line, to keep step; “let us walk by the same rule” (Php 3:16).
Greek ktisis (G2937) — a creation, a creature; “but a new creature” (Gal 6:15).
Greek doulagogeo (G1396) — to bring into bondage as a servant; “and bring it into subjection” (1Co 9:27).
usage: “peace be on them, and mercy” (Gal 6:16) — a benediction on rule-keepers of one kind.
“let us mind the same thing” (Php 3:16) — the rule is agreement, not uniformity of dress.
“lest that by any means” (1Co 9:27) — apostolic self-discipline, with its reason.

pos: n. (the holding of two or more church benefices at once by one man, with the duties of all but one discharged by a deputy or not at all)
etymology: From Latin pluralis, of more than one; the ecclesiastical sense is distinct from the modern philosophical and religious senses of the word.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastical pluralism is the holding of several livings at once. A man might be rector of three parishes, prebendary of a cathedral and archdeacon besides, drawing the income of all and residing in none, with curates paid a pittance to do the work. It was the standing abuse of the English church from the thirteenth century until the reforms of the eighteen-thirties, and it was repeatedly condemned by councils, repeatedly dispensed by popes and bishops, and never stopped until Parliament stopped it. The Lord settled the question of divided service in a sentence that is about money and is exactly applicable here: “No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). And the shepherd whose own the sheep are not behaves predictably when anything costs him: “he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pluralist as a clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one with cure of souls; and plurality as the holding of two or more benefices by the same clergyman.
webster_full: PLURALIST, n. A clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one, with cure of souls.
PLURALITY, n. In the church of England, a plurality of benefices, where the same clergyman holds two or more.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
NON-RESIDENCE, n. The omission of residence on a benefice; the neglect of residing where official duties require.
CURE, n. Spiritual charge; the care of souls; the oversight of a parish.
scriptures: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
corruption_summary: One man holding three livings and residing in none, the standing abuse of the English church for six centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is total and was always known to be. Every council that condemned pluralism was attended by pluralists; every dispensation that permitted it was granted by an authority that had condemned it; and the men who benefited were often sincerely devout. That is what makes it instructive. A system can be understood by everyone to be wrong and continue for six hundred years because the alternative costs the people who would have to change it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a cure of souls is a cure of particular souls who can be named. Ezekiel's charge against the shepherds is a list of omissions — “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken” (Eze 34:4) — and omissions are what a man in another county necessarily commits. The hireling is defined not by taking wages but by what he does when the wolf comes, since he “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).
roots_summary: Latin pluralis, more than one; Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve as a slave; Greek mamonas (G3126), mammon or wealth; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Hebrew chalah (H2470), to be sick.
roots_lines: Latin pluralis — of more than one; the ecclesiastical sense is a term of art.
Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).
Greek mamonas (G3126) — wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24).
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired man; “he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd” (Joh 10:12).
Greek melo (G3199) — to care for; “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).
usage: “or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other” (Mat 6:24) — the arithmetic of three livings.
“and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12) — what the deputy system produces.
“neither have ye bound up that which was broken” (Eze 34:4) — omission, the absentee's sin.

pos: n. (the holding of land by a corporation, especially a religious house, in perpetuity — literally the dead hand, because such land never falls back to the lord by death or marriage)
etymology: Anglo-French morte main, dead hand, from Latin mortua manus — land gripped by a hand that never dies and never lets go.
biblical_def: Mortmain is the medieval name for land held by a body that does not die. A corporation has no heir, no minority, no marriage and no death, so the feudal incidents by which a lord recovered value from his tenants never fell due, and land granted to a monastery was effectively out of the system for ever. The Statute of Mortmain of 1279 forbade such grants without royal licence, and the phrase has passed into the law of charity, where it still describes the grip of a long-dead donor's instructions on a living institution. The image is exact and Scripture has its own version. The law of Israel refused permanent alienation outright, resetting every holding in the fiftieth year: “ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession” (Lev 25:10). The jubilee is precisely an anti-mortmain statute, and its ground is that the land is God's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mortmain as possession of lands or tenements in dead hands, or hands that cannot alienate; and alienate as to transfer title, property or right to another.
webster_full: MORTMAIN, n. In law, possession of lands or tenements in dead hands, or hands that cannot alienate. Alienation in mortmain is an alienation of lands or tenements to any corporation, sole or aggregate, ecclesiastical or temporal.
ALIENATE, v.t. To transfer title, property or right to another; as, to alienate lands or sovereignty.
CORPORATION, n. A body politic or corporate, formed and authorized by law to act as a single person.
PERPETUITY, n. Endless duration; continued uninterrupted existence. The quality or condition of an estate by which it becomes inalienable.

JUBILEE, n. Among the Jews, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all the slaves were liberated, and all lands which had been alienated during the whole period, reverted to their former owners.
scriptures: And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.
Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.
Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
corruption_summary: The dead hand: land held for ever by a body that never dies, and the jubilee that was designed to prevent it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the permanent grip of the past on the present, which is a danger to churches and charities and not only to feudal lords. An endowment made in 1280 for masses nobody now believes in still determines what a building may be used for; a trust deed written in one century governs a congregation in another. Our Lord's sharpest word about obligations owed to the dead is addressed to a man with a genuinely pressing claim: “Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:60).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the jubilee's reason, which is not economic policy but ownership: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). No hand holds anything for ever because no hand owns it. The Preacher adds the builder's own frustration, that a man must leave his work “unto the man that shall be after me” (Ecc 2:18) and cannot know what he will do with it.
roots_summary: Anglo-French morte main, dead hand; Hebrew yobel (H3104), a jubilee; Hebrew deror (H1865), liberty; Hebrew achuzzah (H272), a possession; Hebrew ger (H1616), a sojourner.
roots_lines: Anglo-French morte main — the dead hand, Latin mortua manus.
Hebrew yobel (H3104) — a ram's horn, the jubilee year; “it shall be a jubile unto you” (Lev 25:10).
Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, release; “proclaim liberty throughout all the land” (Lev 25:10).
Hebrew achuzzah (H272) — a possession, a holding; “return every man unto his possession” (Lev 25:10).
Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a resident alien; “ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23).
usage: “and ye shall return every man unto his family” (Lev 25:10) — the statute against the dead hand.
“for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23) — why no grip is permanent.
“but go thou and preach the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:60) — the living claim outranks the dead.

pos: n. (free alms: a tenure by which a church or religious house held land of a donor with no secular service due, the only return being prayer for the donor and his heirs)
etymology: Anglo-French franke almoigne, free alms, from franc, free, and almoigne, alms — land given in free alms.
biblical_def: Frankalmoin was the commonest tenure by which English religious houses held land. The donor granted a manor or a church in liberam elemosinam, in free alms; no rent, no knight service and no suit of court were owed, and the only return specified was spiritual — prayers, masses, and the donor's name in the house's calendar. The law courts took the tenure seriously enough that the remedy for a lapse was not seizure of the land but a complaint to the bishop. The arrangement rests on a genuine duty wrongly priced. Prayer for others, including for the powerful, is commanded: “that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1), and specifically “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). Jeremiah commanded the exiles to pray for a pagan city, “for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7). What is nowhere commanded is that such prayer be owed as rent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frankalmoigne as free alms, a tenure by which a religious corporation holds lands to them and their successors for ever, on condition of praying for the soul of the donor; and intercession as prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
webster_full: FRANKALMOIGNE, n. Free alms; in English law, a tenure by which a religious corporation holds lands to them and their successors forever, on condition of praying for the soul of the donor.
INTERCESSION, n. The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
TENURE, n. The manner of holding lands or tenements of a superior.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor; a charitable gift.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship.
scriptures: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
corruption_summary: Land held in free alms for prayers alone, and the duty of intercession turned into rent.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is prayer as consideration in a contract. Once intercession is the service by which land is held, the transaction has a price, a term and a remedy for breach, and the prayers are owed to a man rather than offered to God on his behalf. The slide from gift to obligation is invisible in the charters themselves, which are warm and pious documents; it shows in what happened when houses stopped keeping the obits and donors' families went to law.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that intercession is a mutual duty of the whole church with no fee attached: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jam 5:16). The power is located in righteousness and fervency, neither of which can be bought, and the direction is one for another, which is not a tenure.
roots_summary: Anglo-French franke almoigne, free alms; Greek enteuxis (G1783), intercession; Greek deesis (G1162), supplication; Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace; Greek energeo (G1754), to work effectually.
roots_lines: Anglo-French franke almoigne — free alms; Latin libera elemosina.
Greek enteuxis (G1783) — a petition, an intercession; “supplications, prayers, intercessions” (1Ti 2:1).
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness; “in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2).
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, welfare; “seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7).
Greek energeo (G1754) — to be operative, to work effectually; “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jam 5:16).
usage: “that, first of all” (1Ti 2:1) — intercession given priority, not price.
“and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7) — commanded for a city that had enslaved them.
“pray one for another” (Jam 5:16) — mutual, and not a tenure.

pos: n. (the great barn in which a parish's tithe paid in kind — sheaves, wool, cheese — was stored for the rector or the monastery that had appropriated the living)
etymology: Old English teotha, a tenth, with bere-aern, a barley house — the barn for the tenth.
biblical_def: A tithe barn is one of the largest buildings a medieval village ever saw, and some of them — Great Coxwell, Bradford-on-Avon, Tisbury — are cathedrals of timber and stone built to hold grain. The tithe was paid in kind, and it had to be stored, so wherever a monastery had appropriated a parish it raised a barn to take the tenth sheaf out of that parish's fields. The buildings are magnificent and the arrangement was resented, because the grain left the village. The storehouse is a biblical object and carries a biblical promise: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing” (Mal 3:10). The prophet's stated purpose for the tithe is that there be meat in God's house, which is to say that the Levites eat and the poor are fed; a barn that exports the tenth to a distant abbey has kept the form and moved the purpose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tithe as the tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy; and barn as a covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
webster_full: TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support.
BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
GARNER, n. A granary; a building or place where grain is stored for preservation.
APPROPRIATE, v.t. In ecclesiastical affairs, to annex, as a benefice, to a spiritual corporation, as its perpetual property.
STOREHOUSE, n. A house in which things are stored; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
scriptures: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field.
corruption_summary: The great barn built to hold a parish's tenth, which a distant abbey then carried away.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is appropriation: the tenth of a village's harvest leaving the village. Nehemiah found the same failure in Jerusalem and dealt with it as an administrative scandal, because “the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field” (Neh 13:10). When the maintenance does not reach the men who do the work, the work stops; and a parish served by an underpaid vicar out of a barn full of its own grain is Nehemiah's situation in English.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a full barn is not itself a sign of blessing, and the Lord told a parable about a man who built bigger ones. “I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods” (Luk 12:18) is answered the same night: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Luk 12:20). The Great Coxwell barn still stands and its owners are all dead.
roots_summary: Old English teotha, a tenth; Hebrew maaser (H4643), a tithe; Hebrew otsar (H214), a treasury or storehouse; Hebrew bachan (H974), to test or prove; Greek apotheke (G596), a barn or granary.
roots_lines: Old English teotha + bere-aern — the tenth, and the barley house.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tenth; “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse” (Mal 3:10).
Hebrew otsar (H214) — a store, a treasury; the storehouse of Malachi.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to prove; “and prove me now herewith” (Mal 3:10).
Greek apotheke (G596) — a storehouse, a barn; “I will pull down my barns, and build greater” (Luk 12:18).
usage: “that there may be meat in mine house” (Mal 3:10) — the stated purpose of the tenth.
“were fled every one to his field” (Neh 13:10) — what unpaid ministers do.
“then whose shall those things be” (Luk 12:20) — asked of every great barn.
